pieces.title: Aria · BWV 988
pieces.note: Hear the bass descend under the ornamented opening. Its harmonic course will hold the thirty variations together.

pieces.title: Variation 1 · BWV 988
pieces.note: A short figure passes from one hand to the other over the three-beat pulse. Follow its changing register.

pieces.title: Variation 2 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Two strands of imitation move over a separate bass. Choose a short turn in the upper parts and follow the answer.

pieces.title: Variation 3 · Canon at the unison · BWV 988
pieces.note: The second voice enters on the same pitch level as the first. A separate bass supports the canon.

pieces.title: Variation 4 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Listen for the brief opening figure answering itself across registers in a light three-beat dance.

pieces.title: Variation 5 · BWV 988
pieces.note: The quick line and the wide jumps trade hands. Follow the long leaps against the succession of short notes.

pieces.title: Variation 6 · Canon at the second · BWV 988
pieces.note: The entering voice takes up the melody at the interval of a second. Follow the first two entries over the bass.

pieces.title: Variation 7 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Bach marked this variation al tempo di giga. Listen for the dotted lilt and the two groups of three in each bar.

pieces.title: Variation 8 · BWV 988
pieces.note: A two-manual piece. Listen to the changes of register as the short runs pass between the hands.

pieces.title: Variation 9 · Canon at the third · BWV 988
pieces.note: A canon at the third. Sing the leader’s opening and follow the answering line at a different pitch.

pieces.title: Variation 10 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Bach calls this a Fughetta. The opening subject gathers new voices until there are four sounding parts.

pieces.title: Variation 11 · BWV 988
pieces.note: The two hands exchange quick figures over a lilting pulse. Notice how one hand sustains the motion as the other changes register.

pieces.title: Variation 12 · Canon at the fourth · BWV 988
pieces.note: A canon at the fourth in contrary motion. Where the leading line rises, its answer falls.

pieces.title: Variation 13 · BWV 988
pieces.note: A decorated upper line unfolds over a steady bass. Trace the melody through the smaller notes that ornament it.

pieces.title: Variation 14 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Short attacks and sudden leaps give this two-manual variation its bite. Watch for the change of register.

pieces.title: Variation 15 · Canon at the fifth · BWV 988
pieces.note: The first variation in G minor is a canon at the fifth in contrary motion. The second voice turns the first voice’s contour upside down.

pieces.title: Variation 16 · Ouverture · BWV 988
pieces.note: The second half of the cycle opens like a French overture. Broad dotted figures lead to a much quicker imitative section.

pieces.title: Variation 17 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Following the weight of the overture, two quick lines trade places across the keyboard.

pieces.title: Variation 18 · Canon at the sixth · BWV 988
pieces.note: A canon at the sixth. Follow the two imitating lines while the independent bass keeps its own pattern.

pieces.title: Variation 19 · BWV 988
pieces.note: An unhurried three-part dance in 3/8. Trace the short opening rhythm as it moves through the texture.

pieces.title: Variation 20 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Listen for the shifting register as running notes pass from one hand to the other. The bass landmarks remain those of the Aria.

pieces.title: Variation 21 · Canon at the seventh · BWV 988
pieces.note: The canon at the seventh returns to G minor. Hear the chromatic motion in the bass under the two imitating voices.

pieces.title: Variation 22 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Bach marks this variation alla breve. Listen for the opening bass pattern under its measured, contrapuntal texture.

pieces.title: Variation 23 · BWV 988
pieces.note: The hands pursue each other with short, nimble figures. Listen for the exchanges before their parts overlap.

pieces.title: Variation 24 · Canon at the octave · BWV 988
pieces.note: A canon at the octave in 9/8. Listen for the answer in a different register against the rocking groups of three.

pieces.title: Variation 25 · BWV 988
pieces.note: An Adagio in G minor. The upper melody leans on dissonant notes while the bass moves by small chromatic steps.

pieces.title: Variation 26 · BWV 988
pieces.note: A running figure and a slower sarabande rhythm coexist. Follow one layer as the hands exchange them.

pieces.title: Variation 27 · Canon at the ninth · BWV 988
pieces.note: This canon at the ninth has just its two imitating parts. Hear how the bass of the cycle is suggested within them.

pieces.title: Variation 28 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Trills run through the movement. Listen beneath their repeated alternation for the larger shape of the line.

pieces.title: Variation 29 · BWV 988
pieces.note: Firmly struck chords and rapid figures alternate. The contrast in density is audible even at a slower playback speed.

pieces.title: Variation 30 · Quodlibet · BWV 988
pieces.note: The Quodlibet combines familiar song melodies above the Aria’s bass. After it, return to the opening Aria.

composers.name: Joseph-Nicolas-Pancrace Royer
composers.note: Royer published his Premier livre de pièces de clavecin in Paris in 1746. Several pieces recall his work for the stage.

composers.name: Jehan Titelouze
composers.note: Organist of Rouen Cathedral. His 1623 collection sets plainchant hymns in organ versets for alternation with singing.

guides.Goldberg Variations: Start with the Aria and listen for its bass in a variation. A canon appears every third variation up to No. 27. Each one widens the interval between the entering voices.
guides.Keyboard partitas: The dances in a partita share a key but change step, meter and pace. Nos. 3 and 6 here use the early versions in Anna Magdalena Bach’s 1725 notebook. The source for No. 2 includes its first two movements.
guides.The Well-Tempered Clavier: In each book Bach paired a prelude with a fugue in each of the 24 major and minor keys. In a fugue, learn the opening subject and listen for its return in another register.
guides.Preludes, fantasias and fugues: Bach’s short preludes concentrate on a figure that fits under the hand. The longer fantasias allow a subject to give way to running passages and chords.
guides.Keyboard toccatas: Sections change scale and character within a single work. Follow the movement from free flourishes into a fugue whose subject passes between voices.
guides.Italian Concerto: Bach wrote a concerto for a solo two-manual harpsichord. Listen to the changing density as a full ensemble and a soloist seem to answer each other.
guides.Music for lute: A plucked string soon dies away. Listen for how broken chords and small changes in the bass keep the harmony sounding across the gaps.
guides.Sonatas and partitas for solo violin: Bach’s three sonatas and three partitas put melody, bass and chords within a single violin part. The room renders the notes on piano. A double is a decorated partner to the dance before it.
guides.Suites for solo cello: Bach places a prelude before a sequence of dances. In each suite the two minuets offer a close comparison of register, rhythm and phrase.
guides.Aylesford pieces: These short keyboard pieces survive together in the Aylesford collection. Try two minuets side by side and follow the same three-beat step through different keys.
guides.Nine German Arias: Handel set texts by Barthold Heinrich Brockes for voice, an obbligato instrument and continuo. Follow the dialogue between the obbligato and the sung line above the bass.
guides.Handel on stage: An aria often states its mood through the instruments before the singer enters. Open the source score for the text and compare the first vocal phrase with the introduction.
guides.The Four Seasons: Four violin concertos make a year. Each has three movements. In the source score the solo violin emerges from the string ensemble to give individual scenes a voice.
guides.L’estro armonico: The first six concertos from Vivaldi’s Op. 3 alternate combinations of solo strings. Listen for music passed between the soloists and the return of the ensemble.
guides.The French harpsichord: Couperin’s teaching preludes explore touch and timing. Royer’s 1746 Premier livre brings songs, character pieces and dances from the stage to the keyboard.
guides.French organ versets: An organist and singers could alternate verses of a plainchant hymn. These versets by Titelouze are the organ’s side of that exchange.
guides.Membra Jesu nostri: Buxtehude’s cycle follows seven Latin meditations, from Ad pedes to Ad faciem. The contrast between instrumental passages, solo arias and ensemble singing remains audible in the piano rendering.
guides.Chamber and organ music: The scores range from music for a single flutist to an ensemble of violins. Check the original instrumentation in the edition when comparing what the same lines sound like on piano.
